newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Swedish Riksbank sees no need to move repo rate.
newsitem.headline: Swedish Riksbank sees no need to move repo rate.

text.p: The governor of Sweden's central bank, Urban Backstrom, said on Wednesday that there was no need to change the key repurchase rate at the present time.
"On the whole, economic tendencies confirm the picture in the Riksbank's latest inflation report," Backstrom said in a speech he gave in southern Sweden, a copy of which was released in Stockholm.
"So at present we see no need to alter the repo rate," he said.
The Riksbank cut the repo in stages last year to 4.10 percent from 8.91 percent, but has not moved it in 1997.
Regarding the Swedish economy, Backstrom mentioned high unemployment, 8.4 percent in March, as a negative factor.
"Most of the evidence suggests that unemployment has become structural, which means that, unless measures are taken, it is liable to remain high even if activity continues to improve," he said.
This indicates that the labour market is functioning poorly, partly on account of wage formation since this is the central market mechanism, he said.
Backstrom called for measures to reduce the structural causes of unemployment but said: "That, however, is not a matter for demand policy, that is, fiscal and monetary policy."
"What monetary policy could do is try to keep inflation low and stable as an indirect contribution to stable growth," he said.

In addition, Sweden still has higher long bond yields than other European countries and the crown has softened in recent months so the need for disciplined economic policy remains unchanged, Backstrom said.
On the other hand, Backstrom said the Swedish economy displayed many favourable tendencies, noting low inflation and increased growth.
"It seems that Sweden's economy is entering a period of increased growth," he said.
"Everything suggests that the economy has unutilised resources, so in the near future there should not be any crucial capacity restrictions.

"And if households and firms continue to count on low inflation when making economic decisions, there is a good prospect of price increases remaining low in 1997 and 1998, which is the period we can assess at present."
